title: Build and Evaluate a Rule
background:
The `Rule` class in *JsonLogic* represents a computation. You build rules from operators and values, then evaluate them to produce a result.

The `JsonLogic` class provides static factory methods that return typed `Rule` objects. Primitive C# values such as `int`, `decimal`, `bool`, and `string` implicitly convert to `Rule` via conversion operators defined on the `Rule` base class, so you can pass literals directly to factory methods without calling `JsonLogic.Literal` explicitly.
instructions: Build a rule that adds the `a` and `b` test values, then return the result of `rule.Apply()`.

title: Apply a Rule to Data
background:
Rules can read values from an input document by using `JsonLogic.Variable(...)` and then evaluating the rule with `rule.Apply(data)`. This is the basic pattern for data-driven evaluation in *JsonLogic*.

You can still compose the rule with typed factory methods in C#. Primitive C# values implicitly convert to `Rule` via `LiteralRule`, so literals and variable rules can be combined directly.
instructions: Build a rule that uses `JsonLogic.Variable("age")` and returns `true` only when age is greater than 18 and less than 65, then apply it to the provided `data`.

title: Rule Deserialization
background:
Rules stored as JSON strings — in a database, config file, or API response — can be deserialized directly to a typed `Rule` using `System.Text.Json`. The library registers a `JsonConverter<Rule>` (`LogicComponentConverter`) that handles the conversion. A single-key JSON object is read as an operator rule; a multi-key object or primitive becomes a `LiteralRule`; a JSON array becomes a `RuleCollection`.

Once deserialized, the `Rule` is a first-class typed object you can evaluate with `rule.Apply(data)`, inspect, or serialize back to JSON. This makes it straightforward to load rules from any storage format and execute them in a strongly-typed context.
instructions: Deserialize `test["rule"]` to a typed `Rule`, then apply it to `test["data"]`.

title: Variable Paths and Fallbacks
background:
`JsonLogic.Variable(string path)` can read nested values using dot-delimited paths such as `"profile.city"`. When a path cannot be resolved, the rule returns `null`.

`JsonLogic.Variable(string path, Rule defaultValue)` lets you provide a fallback value for missing paths. This is useful when input documents are incomplete and you want a predictable output instead of `null`.
instructions: Build a variable lookup rule for `profile.city` with a default of `"unknown"`, then apply it to the test data.

title: Truthiness
background:
*JsonLogic* defines truthiness through the `IsTruthy()` extension method on `JsonNode?` (in the `Json.Logic` namespace). These rules drive the behavior of `And`, `Or`, `Not`, `If`, and other conditional operators throughout the library.

The falsey values are: `null`, `false`, `0`, `""` (empty string), `[]` (empty array), and `{}` (empty object). The empty object being falsey is a difference from JavaScript that is worth noting when passing objects through conditional rules.
instructions: Return whether `test["value"]` is truthy using the `IsTruthy()` extension method.

title: Strict vs Loose Equality
background:
*JsonLogic* provides two equality modes. `JsonLogic.StrictEquals` (the `===` operator) compares by both type and value: the number `1` and the string `"1"` are not equal. `JsonLogic.LooseEquals` (the `==` operator) coerces values through `Numberify` before comparing: `"1"` is parsed as `1`, making them equal.

Choosing the wrong mode is a common source of integration bugs. Strict equality is the safer default when you control the data shape. Loose equality is useful when rules may receive mixed types from external sources — for example, form fields that arrive as strings — and numeric equivalence is the intended comparison.
instructions: Build an equality rule that uses strict comparison when `test["strict"]` is `true` and loose comparison otherwise, using `a` and `b` from the test. Apply it with no data.

title: Numeric Coercion
background:
The arithmetic operators in *JsonLogic* — `Add`, `Subtract`, `Multiply`, `Divide`, `Modulus`, `Max`, and `Min` — pass each operand through a `Numberify()` conversion before computing. `Numberify` converts: `true` → `1`, `false` → `0`, `null` → `0`, parseable numeric strings like `"3"` → `3`, and non-parseable strings → `null` (which short-circuits the result to `null`).

This means that rules operating on data from external sources — where a field might be `"5"` or `5` depending on the sender — produce consistent arithmetic results without requiring the caller to normalize types in advance.
instructions: Build a numeric rule that sums `test["a"]` and `test["b"]`, then return the result of `rule.Apply()`.

title: Rule Tree Serialization
background:
Every typed `Rule` built with the *JsonLogic* factory methods supports round-trip serialization. The `LogicComponentConverter` registered on `Rule` writes it back to its original operator-and-arguments JSON form. Deserializing that JSON with `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Rule>()` reconstructs an equivalent rule that evaluates identically.

This makes typed rules suitable for storage, caching, and transport. You can build a rule in C#, serialize it to a string, store it, load it back, and evaluate it — all without losing fidelity. The same `System.Text.Json` options apply throughout, so no extra configuration is needed.
instructions: Serialize `rule` to JSON, deserialize it back to a typed `Rule`, then apply the deserialized rule to `test["data"]`.

title: Unknown Operator Behavior
background:
The two evaluation paths in *JsonLogic* handle unknown operators differently. The model-less path — `JsonLogic.Apply(JsonNode? rule, ...)` — silently returns the original rule node unchanged when no handler is registered for the operator. The typed deserialization path — `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Rule>(...)` — throws a `JsonException` immediately at deserialization time because the converter cannot map the operator string to a registered `Rule` type.

This distinction matters when building integration code that accepts rules from external sources. The typed path fails fast and is straightforward to reason about; the model-less path is permissive and requires you to inspect the result if you need to detect unrecognized operators.
instructions: Try to deserialize `test["rule"]` as a `Rule` and apply it to `test["data"]`. Catch `JsonException` and return `null` if the operator is unknown.

title: Custom Operators
background:
*JsonLogic* lets you add new operators by implementing the `IRule` interface — a single `Apply(JsonNode? args, EvaluationContext context)` method — and registering an instance with `RuleRegistry.AddRule(string op, IRule rule)`. Once registered, any evaluation that encounters that operator name will dispatch to your handler.

Inside the handler, `args` is the raw JSON argument from the rule. You can call `JsonLogic.Apply(args, context)` to evaluate it recursively, which allows your operator to accept nested rules as arguments just like the built-in operators do.
instructions: Implement an `IRule` handler for a `"double"` operator that multiplies its evaluated argument by 2, then register it in the rule registry before evaluation.
